title: Save the burning world
hook: the world is burning; save it by whatever door it can be saved (Bilaval Var M3, ang 853)

segments.voice: Yesterday: man too jot saroop hai. O mind, you are the form of light; know your origin. Your line was you are light. Did you answer a put-down with it? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

A house is on fire. Smoke at the windows, people inside. Nobody standing on the lawn holds a meeting about which door is the proper one. Front door, back door, a ladder at the upstairs window: whichever opening gets someone out is the right one. Yesterday, Guru Amar Das spoke to the single mind and told it that it was made of light. Today the camera pulls all the way back. In a salok in the Var of Raga Bilaval, he looks at the whole world, sees it burning, and asks for it to be saved by any door at all.
screen: `A HOUSE ON FIRE.` → `WHICHEVER DOOR GETS THEM OUT.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, BURNING.`

segments.voice: The salok, paraphrased: the world is burning; save it, Lord, by Your mercy. By whatever door it can be rescued, rescue it that way. Then it goes on: the True Guru shows the way of peace, through reflecting on the true Word, and Nanak knows no other who forgives. Three things are worth slowing down for. First, who's being asked. This is a prayer addressed to God. It isn't a project plan for heroes. The rescuing is in the Lord's hands, and the Guru is the one asking. Second, what's burning. Some readers hear the fire as an inner one: craving, anger, ego. In that reading, the burning world is a world on fire from the inside. Third, the phrase at the center: by whatever door. Jit duarai. The salok doesn't name a single entrance and close the others. It asks for mercy through whichever door will work. Sikhs read that phrase in more than one way. Some hear a wide generosity: the Guru wants everyone rescued and doesn't haggle over how. Others hear it as the Lord's freedom: God knows which door suits each person, and the asking leaves that choice to God. Some hold both. Either way, the shape of the prayer is open-handed. A prayer like that leaves a question for whoever says it: is there a door I could open myself? That's today's line.
screen: `A PRAYER, NOT A PLAN.` · `A FIRE FROM THE INSIDE.` · `JIT DUARAI: BY WHATEVER DOOR.` · `READ AS GENEROSITY, OR GOD'S FREEDOM.` · then, large: `BY ANY DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help at any door. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who seems to be burning a little right now: stressed, grieving, stuck. Don't plan a rescue. Just ask yourself which door is open to you. A message. A meal. A quiet stretch of listening. A ride. Let one door come clear and rest there. If you pray, you can hold that person in the words of the salok: save them by whatever door they can be saved. The bell holds the time.
Save the burning world. Guru Amar Das's prayer in Raga Bilaval: the world is burning; by Your mercy, save it, by whatever door it can be saved. Today's word.
Your line: by any door. Today, walk through the one door you found in the sit, even if it's a small one. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.
